job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here's a section-by-section read. I've flagged everything that looks like a gap, ambiguity, or drafting defect; a few are arguably deliberate policy choices rather than errors, so I've noted where that's likely so your coverage can distinguish the two. I'm working only from the text you pasted, so please check it against the committee print before publication.

**Section 2 — Definitions**

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — Per-vessel threshold invites fleet-splitting.** The 10,000-ton trigger is measured "by a single vessel," so an operator can run several vessels each just under the cap with no aggregation across a fleet, operator, or project. Nothing attributes tonnage to affiliates, charterers, or a common owner.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "Per year" is undefined.** Calendar year, 12-month rolling period, or license year? An operator could also reset the clock by swapping vessels mid-year or transferring a vessel to a new operator.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — No weight basis specified.** Nodules can be weighed wet or dry, with or without sediment; the difference is large enough to move an operation across the threshold, and the bill gives no measurement standard or who verifies it.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — Activity below the threshold is simply not "mining."** Because the threshold is built into the definition rather than an exemption, recovering up to 10,000 tons per vessel per year is fully lawful with no permit, review, or reporting beyond Sec. 4's thin registry.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — Only "recovery" is covered.** Transporting, processing, refining, selling, importing, financing, insuring, or supplying equipment for seabed minerals is untouched, so a U.S. company can contract with a foreign operator and take delivery of the output.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "Other mineral resources" is undefined and potentially overbroad.** Read literally it could reach deepwater oil and gas, sand/gravel, or sediment removal below 200 meters, giving opponents a strong "unintended consequences" argument and courts a reason to construe the whole definition narrowly.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — "The Secretary" is never defined.** No section identifies which Secretary (Commerce, Interior, State?) makes the determination; this is a plain drafting error that leaves the provision inoperable or litigable.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — Open-ended administrative definition of a felony.** The Secretary may declare "any activity" with "comparable" risks to be prohibited conduct carrying 10 years' imprisonment, with no rulemaking procedure, notice, standards, or judicial-review provision. Expect vagueness, nondelegation, and rule-of-lenity challenges, and overbreadth objections that it could sweep in cable-laying, research, or bottom trawling.

9. **Sec. 2(2) — "U.S. person" omits most entity types.** Only citizens and "corporations" organized under a "State" are covered; LLCs, partnerships, trusts, nonprofits, lawful permanent residents, and entities organized in DC, Puerto Rico, or other territories ("State" is undefined) are arguably outside it.

10. **Sec. 2(2) — No foreign-subsidiary or control test.** A U.S. parent can conduct mining through a subsidiary incorporated abroad (the Nauru/Tonga sponsorship model already in use) and fall outside the prohibition entirely; there is no "owned or controlled by" language of the kind used in sanctions and export-control statutes.

11. **Sec. 2(3) — Covered-vessel definition has gaps and no nexus.** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less escape the registry entirely; "equipped for the recovery" is undefined (support ships? vessels carrying detachable collectors?); and the definition has no flag or ownership tie, so it purports to cover every such vessel in the world while providing no practical way to compel foreign-flag compliance.

12. **Sec. 2 — Missing definitions generally.** "Person," "vessel," "seabed," "recovery," "operator," "exploration license," "United States," and "State" are all undefined, each of which matters to the scope of a criminal statute.

**Section 3 — Prohibition**

13. **Sec. 3(a) — No flag-state hook.** The prohibition reaches "persons in the United States" and "U.S. persons anywhere" but not U.S.-flagged vessels; flag jurisdiction is the most robust basis for high-seas enforcement, and its absence lets a foreign operator use a U.S.-documented vessel.

14. **Sec. 3(a) — "In the United States" may not reach the EEZ or outer continental shelf.** Whether the U.S. EEZ (where seabed below 200 m exists) is "in the United States" is a genuine question with no definition to answer it, so a foreign company mining in U.S. waters beyond the territorial sea may not be covered.

15. **Sec. 3(a) — No aiding, abetting, conspiracy, or attempt liability.** General federal accomplice law (18 U.S.C. § 2) may fill part of the criminal gap, but the civil penalty applies only to one who "violates section 3," leaving facilitators, financiers, and charterers unreachable.

16. **Sec. 3(a) — Silent on existing statutes.** The bill neither amends nor repeals the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. § 1401 et seq.), under which NOAA retains authority to issue commercial recovery permits, nor OCSLA; the conflict invites implied-repeal litigation and leaves the permitting machinery the bill is meant to stop legally intact.

17. **Sec. 3(b) — Grandfather clause is broad and permanent.** "Mining conducted under an exploration license" is undefined: it does not say who the issuer must be (NOAA, the ISA, or any foreign state), has no end date, and does not address renewals, extensions, amendments, assignments, or conversion to exploitation contracts after enactment. A license issued the day before enactment could shelter commercial-scale extraction indefinitely.

18. **Sec. 3(b) — Creates a race to license.** Because the cutoff is enactment rather than introduction or committee action, there is a clear incentive for applicants and issuing authorities to push licenses out before the President signs.

19. **Sec. 3(c) — Purpose-based exemption with no limits.** Activity "for the purpose of environmental assessment" is exempt regardless of tonnage, duration, or who conducts it, with no agency approval, scale cap, or data-sharing requirement; an operator can characterize large collector trials as assessment, and purpose is hard to disprove.

20. **Sec. 3(c) vs. Sec. 2(1)(B) — Internal tension.** The Secretary could deem assessment activity "comparable" in risk under (1)(B), yet (c) exempts it; the bill doesn't say which controls.

**Section 4 — Registry**

21. **Sec. 4 — No penalty for noncompliance.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of Section 3, so failing to register, failing to report, or filing a false report carries no sanction under this Act (18 U.S.C. § 1001 may apply to false certifications, but nothing compels filing).

22. **Sec. 4(a) — No deadline or content requirements.** The bill does not say when registration is due, what information it must include, or whether NOAA may issue rules to implement it.

23. **Sec. 4(b) — Reports don't require the data needed to enforce.** Operators must "describe" recovery activities but are not required to report tonnage, location, depth, or dates — the exact facts needed to establish a 10,000-ton violation — and NOAA is given no inspection, audit, boarding, or verification authority.

**Section 5 — Penalties**

24. **Sec. 5(a) — Per-day penalty doesn't fit an annual-tonnage violation.** The offense is defined by exceeding a yearly total, so it's unclear on which "day" a violation "occurs": only the day the threshold is crossed, every day thereafter in the year, or every day of recovery retroactively. This will be litigated.

25. **Sec. 5(a) — Conflicts with Sec. 8.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act doesn't take effect until 180 days later; read literally this either penalizes lawful pre-effective conduct (due process / ex post facto problem) or is meaningless.

26. **Sec. 5 — No enforcement mechanism.** No agency is designated to assess penalties, no court or procedure is specified, and there is no injunctive relief, in rem forfeiture, vessel seizure, citizen suit, or inflation adjustment; the civil penalty is also only "not more than" $1 million with no floor or factors.

27. **Sec. 5(b) — "Willfully" plus a vague definition.** The high mens rea standard combined with the undefined terms in Section 2 and the Secretary's discretionary category makes criminal prosecution difficult and strengthens rule-of-lenity defenses.

**Sections 6–8 — International, Duration, Effective Date**

28. **Sec. 6 — Hortatory and ambiguous.** "Shall seek to negotiate" imposes no enforceable obligation, and "not later than 18 months" could modify beginning to seek or concluding the agreement; there is no report to Congress or consequence for inaction.

29. **Sec. 7(a) — Legally inert condition.** A joint resolution is itself a law, so Congress can already repeal the prohibition at any time with or without a National Academies report; the clause purports to bind a future Congress, which it cannot do. "Serious harm" is undefined, and no one is directed or funded to commission the Academies report.

30. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b) — Direct contradiction.** (a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress affirmatively finds mining is safe; (b) says the entire Act ends in 10 years regardless. The sunset will likely control as the more specific provision, which means the bill as written is a time-limited moratorium rather than the prohibition its title suggests — worth flagging to readers.

31. **Sec. 7(b) — Sunset of the whole Act, no savings clause.** Because the registry and penalties also expire, enforcement actions pending at the 10-year mark may be contested (1 U.S.C. § 109 should preserve accrued penalties, but an express savings clause would remove doubt). Measured from enactment while the Act takes effect 180 days later, the operative prohibition is really about 9½ years.

32. **Sec. 8 — Effective-date gap.** The 180-day delay, combined with no interim reporting or registration requirement, gives operators a window to stockpile recovery or restructure operations before the prohibition bites.

**Cross-cutting omissions**

33. **No rulemaking authority, appropriations, or severability clause.** Nothing authorizes any agency to issue implementing regulations or funds enforcement, and without a severability clause a successful challenge to Sec. 2(1)(B) could jeopardize the whole prohibition.

34. **No import or market-access restriction.** Minerals mined by foreign operators can be imported, refined, and sold in the U.S. without restriction, which limits the bill's practical effect on the industry regardless of how the prohibition is drafted.

A note for framing: items 1, 4, 11, 17, and 19 (the tonnage threshold, the 5,000-GT cutoff, the grandfather clause, and the assessment exemption) may reflect negotiated policy choices in the manager's amendment rather than oversights, so it would be fair to ask the sponsors' and committee's staff whether they were intentional before describing them as loopholes. Items 7, 25, and 30 look like straightforward drafting errors.
